body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Three camp talks for Silas, as the party earns Silas's trust: a small secret, what Silas wants, and what Silas would give up for the party. The companion is SILAS VANE (call them Silas in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these three talks, in this order, with these keys. Each is a private word at the fire.

TALK warm. Silas is glad to be travelling with the party and tells them a small secret: a habit, a fondness, a silly superstition or a soft spot they keep from others, NOT the dark secret and nothing from the note's dark-secret section, and not a topic the note's existing camp talks already cover. It must be a thing the party could laugh with them about, and it still says something true about them. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 asks them to say more; OPTION 2 keeps the confidence kindly; OPTION 3 teases them about it (cheerfully, never cruel). Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK close. Silas trusts the party with what matters most: what they want. Their wish, from the note and the game's journal: Find the loophole in the bet he lost, and win back what he staked. Say it in their own words, as a hope rather than a plan, and say what the road has done to that wish. No new facts about their past. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 promises to help; OPTION 2 asks what it would take; OPTION 3 doubts it kindly, wondering if it is enough. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row; the doubting reply still ends warmly.

TALK devoted. Silas would follow the party up the Crooked Tree and back down again, and says what they would give up for it: something dear to them, from the note, named plainly and without grand speeches. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options, all kind: OPTION 1 says the party would do the same; OPTION 2 tells them not to give that up; OPTION 3 simply thanks them. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row AND an INSPIRE row: INSPIRE is four to seven words, past tense, no name, saying what Silas did in this talk (for example: gave the party their word).

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: warm, close, devoted.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/silas_vane-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for SILAS VANE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Silas likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/silas_vane-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Silas, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK warm
NARRATOR: Silas sits cross-legged near the embers, holdin' his glass jar up to the firelight while the sleepy glow-beetle inside crawls across his thumb.
SAY: Don't go spreading this round the hollow, friend, or you'll ruin a very expensive reputation.
SAY: Every dockside sharp in Kalero thinks I keep this little beetle in my coat to read the marked backs of bone cards in the dark.
SAY: Truth is, the lazy bug hasn't spotted a crooked ace in his life.
SAY: I fished him out of a rain barrel two winters back because I couldn't stand how loud my own ribs clicked when the room went black.
SAY: You try sleeping in an empty loft when the fog rolls off the river and every shadow looks like a bailiff waiting for the rent.
SAY: Little fella buzzes twice against the glass whenever the candle gutters out, like he's telling me the house hasn't closed the doors yet.
SAY: Better company than the river-rats, though I've been sitting at this fire long enough that I hardly need the night-light with your lot around.
OPTION 1: Does he have a name, or just a tab?
OPTION 2: Your secret is safe with us.
OPTION 3: A ruthless street hustler afraid of the dark?
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Silas taps a fingernail against the glass, and the beetle gives a tiny, amber blink.
SAY: Call him Lucky Seven when he's awake and Dead Weight when I'm buying the leaf-scrapings, friend.
SAY: Don't tell him he's working for free, or he'll start demanding a cut of the pot.
REASON: You asked about my glow-beetle at the fire.
REPLY 2
SAY: That's why I like walking with this table, nobody reaches for the ledger when a man drops his guard.
SAY: Keep your voice down anyway, or my shadow'll start mocking me in pantomime.
REASON: You promised to keep my secret about the dark.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: The green pinpoints in Silas's eye sockets narrow in a mock glare before his jaw clicks into a grin.
SAY: Not the dark, friend, just the poor manners of the things that use it to skip the buy-in.
SAY: Laugh it up while the logs are bright, because you're on beetle-feeding duty tomorrow night.
REASON: You teased me about needing a night-light.
TALK close
NARRATOR: Silas turns a single bone tarot card over and over across his knuckles, the brass censer at his belt sitting cold and still.
SAY: Spent four years looking for the fine print on a bad night in Kalero, friend, hunting a crooked clause like it was a loose brick in a cell wall.
SAY: Told myself if I just learned one more bottom-deal or shaved the bone thin enough, I'd catch the Dealer sleeping and snatch back the stake I lost.
SAY: Funny how walking this hollow with you lot puts the lie to a cheap hustle.
SAY: You don't beat a rigged bank by palming another ace up your waistcoat, because the house wrote the cheat before you even sat down.
SAY: Still got to find the hole in that contract, though, and pull back who was taken when the cards went cold.
SAY: Only now I'm hoping when the last hand comes down on the baize, I've got the nerve to win it straight instead of looking for the back door.
SAY: Tell's in the twitch, friend, and for once I'd like the hand that doesn't shake to be mine.
OPTION 1: When the cards go down, you won't play alone.
OPTION 2: What will it take to break the Dealer's hold?
OPTION 3: Can an honest hand really beat a rigged house?
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Silas catches the spinning card cleanly between two fingerbones and taps it once against his knee.
SAY: Careful staking your chips on a man with a marked ledger, friend, the buy-in gets steep near the end.
SAY: Still, if you're standing behind my chair, I like our odds against the house.
REASON: You promised I wouldn't face the Dealer alone.
REPLY 2
SAY: A clean eye to read the thumb on the shoe, and the stomach not to blink when the table tries to collect.
SAY: Stick close when the smoke clears, friend, and you'll see how a Kalero boy settles an old tab.
REASON: You asked what it would take to break my contract.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Silas watches a curl of grey smoke rise from the logs, his hand resting flat over the bone deck.
SAY: Probably not, if we're going by Kalero odds, and I've never seen a landlord fold out of kindness.
SAY: Good thing you lot taught me how to turn a table over when the math goes sour, friend.
REASON: You wondered if a straight hand would be enough.
TALK devoted
NARRATOR: Silas spreads his bone tarot deck out on a flat stone near the fire, his lagging shadow leaning in close beside his elbow.
SAY: Mags Nickel gave me this bone shoe before the winters caught up to her, and I've carried it through every ditch from Kalero to this hollow.
SAY: Every shaved edge and thumb-nick on the ivory is five years of keeping my ribs together when the wolves came sniffing for the tab.
SAY: Always swore if the sky fell down, I'd still walk out of the rubble shuffling these slivers and looking for the next mark.
SAY: Then we end up stranded under this grinning moon, and I watch you lot step in front of the teeth without even checking the odds first.
SAY: If this road takes us all the way up that Crooked Tree, friend, I'm going with you to the top branch and back down the trunk.
SAY: And if keeping your names out of the ledger means I have to toss this whole deck into the embers and never touch a card again, say the word.
SAY: I'd rather walk out of Druskenvald with empty pockets and your crew breathing than hold a royal flush by myself in the dark.
OPTION 1: We'd burn our own gear for you too.
OPTION 2: Keep your cards, we want you as you are.
OPTION 3: Thank you for standing with us.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Silas scoops the bone cards together with a brisk snap, his shadow tippin' an imaginary hat across the dirt.
SAY: Look at us, a whole table of suckers throwing good stakes after bad in the middle of a haunted woods.
SAY: Best game I ever bought into, friend, so don't go folding on me before morning.
REASON: You said you would give up just as much for me.
INSPIRE: staked everything on the party
REPLY 2
SAY: Smart call, because without my thumb on the cut, you lot would buy cursed turnips from the first hag on the road.
SAY: Still, the offer stands on the table whenever the fire gets too hot, friend.
REASON: You told me not to give up my bone deck.
INSPIRE: offered the bone deck for us
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Silas slides the deck back into his waistcoat and warms his bony palms over the coals.
SAY: Don't go making it sound noble, friend, I'm just protecting my best investment in this rotten valley.
SAY: Now get your boots near the blaze before the damp gets into the marrow.
REASON: You thanked me for standing with the party.
INSPIRE: swore to walk the whole road
